claims.claim: Fix x in a common open real domain; u and v have finite ordinary two-sided derivatives there. Nonzero increments t tend to zero within that domain. Values u(x),v(x) are constant only with respect to t.
For du=u(x+t)-u(x), dv=v(x+t)-v(x), w=uv, dw=v du+u dv+du dv, hence dw/t=v(du/t)+u(dv/t)+du(dv/t).

lim du/t=u'(x); lim dv/t=v'(x); lim du=lim dv=0 by the already accepted differentiability-implies-continuity lemma. lim v(du/t)=v u'; lim u(dv/t)=u v'; lim du(dv/t)=0*v'=0. All limits are finite and their sum exists.
The finite derivative limit bounds dv/t near zero, so du(dv/t)->0. No factor is divided out. w'=u'v+uv'; the source's uv'+u'v is equivalent.

For finite real constant k and differentiable f at x, k'=0 and (kf)'=0*f+k*f'=k*f'. No division by k; when k=0 the derivative is zero. If f' is undefined, the written RHS is undefined even though the zero function on an open domain is differentiable.
(x/15-3)'=1/15; its increment is t/15 and quotient is 1/15.
Increment t/5 yields quotient 1/5 for every t!=0.
Increment -3t/4 yields quotient -3/4 for every t!=0. The negative sign is preserved.
D=>C has contrapositive not C=>not D. Neither C=>D nor not D=>not C is valid. D denotes finite ordinary differentiability; C denotes continuity at the point.
For |x| at zero, |f(x)-f(0)|=|x| proves continuity with delta=epsilon. The difference quotient is 1 for t>0 and -1 for t<0, so the ordinary derivative at zero does not exist.
